text: A staple is something people use or eat regularly, year after year, without much thinking about it. Rice is a staple food across much of Asia; jeans are a staple of almost every closet. Calling Heinz ketchup a staple means it has sat on kitchen tables for 150 years and never gone out of style. It is spelled the same as the little metal staple that holds paper together, but it is a completely different word.

Something versatile can do many different jobs well instead of being good at only one. A versatile athlete plays several positions; a versatile jacket works in rain and in cold. The cookbooks are making a surprising claim: ketchup is not just for fries, and cooks stir it into curries, spoon it over fish, even bake it into bread.

To inhibit something is to hold it back or slow it down, though not always to stop it completely. Scientists use the word constantly: cold inhibits the growth of mould, and a cast inhibits movement so a broken bone can knit together. Vinegar is sour, and enough of it makes ketchup too acidic for most microbes to grow in, so the sauce keeps for months instead of spoiling in days.

A condiment is a sauce, spread or seasoning you add to food at the table rather than cook into it. Ketchup, mustard, mayonnaise, soy sauce and hot sauce are all condiments. The word covers the whole shelf on the fridge door.

Offal is the organ meat of an animal, the parts that are not muscle: liver, kidneys, heart, tongue. It was ordinary food in Britain and America a century ago and is still common in many countries. The article uses it as a marker of how much eating has changed, since most people today would not want it on their plate.

Jellied eels are a traditional London dish: chopped eel cooked in stock that cools into a wobbly jelly, then eaten cold. It was cheap street food in the East End for over 200 years. Almost nobody eats it now, which is why it appears here alongside offal as a food that has all but disappeared.

Ubiquity means being everywhere at once. If a brand or a song or a phone has ubiquity, you cannot go anywhere without running into it. The ubiquity of Heinz ketchup is the fact that it turns up in restaurants, cafeterias and kitchens all over the world.

To predate something is to have existed before it. The pre- at the front means before, the same pre- as in preview and prehistoric. Saying ketchup long predated Henry J. Heinz means people were making versions of the sauce for a couple of centuries before he was even born.

Fermenting is letting tiny living things such as bacteria or yeast feed on a food and change it, usually making it sour, fizzy or strong-smelling. Yogurt, pickles, bread and soy sauce are all made this way. The original Asian ke-tsiap was fermented fish, meaning the fish was left to break down on purpose until it turned into a salty sauce.
Savoury describes food that tastes salty or meaty rather than sweet: soup, gravy, cheese, roast chicken. It is the opposite of a dessert flavour. Americans usually spell it savory.

Mould is a fuzzy fungus that grows on food that has been left too long, in green, white or black patches. It is the British spelling; Americans write mold. Sauce makers used dark bottles so shoppers could not see the mould floating inside.

A preservative is a chemical added to food to stop it going bad, usually by making it a place where microbes cannot grow. Look at the back of almost any packet in your kitchen and you will find one listed. Heinz made a selling point of leaving them out, which is why the advert insisted his ketchup was NOT drugged.

Sodium benzoate is a white powder added to food and fizzy drinks to keep bacteria and mould from growing. It is still used today and is considered safe in small amounts, but in the 1800s people argued fiercely about whether it belonged in food at all.

Coal tar is the thick black sludge left over when coal is heated in an oven to make fuel and gas. In the 1800s chemists discovered it could be turned into brilliant purples, reds and yellows, and those cheap dyes went into clothes, sweets and sauces. Colouring your ketchup with a by-product of coal is exactly the kind of thing the eat-clean shoppers were worried about.

Today drugged means knocked out by a drug, but in 1876 it meant something different: food that had chemicals secretly stirred into it. An advert shouting NOT DRUGGED was promising shoppers there was nothing hidden in the bottle. It was a real fear at a time when nobody had to list ingredients.

A microbe is a living thing too small to see without a microscope, such as a bacterium, a yeast or a mould. Microbes are what make food spoil: they land on it, feed on it and multiply. Most are harmless and some are useful, but the ones growing in old sauce can make you very sick.

Here signalling does not mean waving or flashing a light. It means showing something about yourself without saying it out loud. A clear glass bottle signalled quality because it let shoppers see there was nothing murky hidden inside, while everyone else was selling sauce in dark glass.

Tangy means having a sharp, mouth-puckering sourness, the way a lemon, a pickle or a sour sweet does. In ketchup the tang comes from the vinegar. The article says that sharpness cuts through greasy dishes, meaning it stops fried food from feeling heavy.

To aver something is to state it firmly, as a fact you are willing to stand behind. It is a formal word, more at home in a courtroom or a newspaper than in conversation. Saying cookbooks aver that ketchup is versatile means the cookbooks state it flatly, not that they merely suggest it.

This is a British article, and in Britain chips are what Americans call french fries: thick hot sticks of fried potato. What Americans call chips, the British call crisps. So chicken nuggets and chips is nuggets and fries, not nuggets and a bag of crisps.

Nostalgia is the warm, slightly aching feeling you get remembering a happier time in your own past. Hearing a song from third grade or smelling a food from a grandparent's kitchen sets it off. Heinz benefits from it because grown-ups reach for the bottle that was on the table when they were seven.

To entrench something is to fix it so firmly in place that shifting it becomes very hard. The word comes from trenches, the deep ditches soldiers dug to hold ground they had taken. Marketing has entrenched Heinz's position, meaning years of advertising have made it the ketchup people assume they want.

A brand is the name and look a company puts on its products so you recognise them instantly: the label, the logo, the shape of the bottle. Two ketchups can taste nearly the same, but only one is a Heinz. A strong brand means people reach for it without comparing.

A pollster is a company that finds out what a population thinks by questioning a carefully chosen small group of people, then using those answers to describe everyone. YouGov is one of the best known. It is how newspapers can report what a whole country believes without asking a whole country.

The default is the option you get when you do not make a choice, like the ringtone a new phone already has. Heinz advertised itself as the default ketchup, meaning the one you buy without thinking about it. You will meet the word constantly in computing, where default settings are the ones nobody changed.

Umpteen is a casual, slightly joking way of saying a lot, too many to bother counting. You might say you have told someone umpteen times. It means there are plenty of rival ketchups on the shelf, not a precise number of them.

An artisan is a skilled worker who makes things by hand in small amounts. On a food label, artisan is meant to signal small-batch and carefully made rather than churned out by a factory, and it usually comes with a higher price. Artisan ketchups are the fancy ones sold beside the ordinary bottle.

To do something in vain is to try hard and get nowhere. The traders tried in vain to recreate the Asian sauce, meaning they kept attempting it and kept failing. You will also hear that someone's effort was not in vain, meaning it did count for something after all.

When food goes off, it spoils and is no longer safe to eat. It is the everyday British way of saying it; Americans usually say goes bad. The same two words mean other things in other sentences, such as an alarm going off, so the food sense comes from the context.

Comfort food is the familiar, filling food that makes you feel looked after, usually because you ate it as a child. Mac and cheese, buttered toast and chicken nuggets are classics. The phrase is about the feeling rather than the flavour.

Staying power is the ability to keep going, or to stay popular, long after other things have faded. A band with staying power still fills stadiums thirty years on. Heinz has it: 150 years and still the bottle on the table.

Henry John Heinz was an American businessman, the son of German immigrants, who started selling food products in Pennsylvania in the 1870s. He launched his tomato ketchup in 1876 and built the company that still carries his name. He was as much a marketer as a cook, famous for the slogan 57 Varieties.

Ke-tsiap was a salty sauce made in Asia from fermented fish, and the word is where ketchup gets its name. It had no tomatoes in it at all. British and Dutch traders met it in the late 1600s, loved it, took the name home and spent the next century failing to copy the taste.

Umami is the savoury, meaty, mouth-filling taste, one of the five basic tastes your tongue can detect alongside sweet, salty, sour and bitter. It comes from a substance called glutamate, which tomatoes, parmesan, soy sauce, mushrooms and cooked meat are all full of. A Japanese chemist named it in 1908; the word means roughly deliciousness.

A prophecy is a prediction about the future. A self-fulfilling prophecy is one that comes true only because people believed it and acted on it. Heinz kept saying it was the ketchup everyone buys, shoppers believed that and bought it, and so it became true.

YouGov is a British research company that surveys people online about products, politics and opinions, then publishes the results. Newspapers quote it constantly. Its figure that 100% of Britons know Heinz comes from questioning a sample of people, not from asking the whole country.

The m here is short for million, so 650m means 650 million. British newspapers write large numbers this way, with bn for billion. It is worth spotting, because a small letter can be the difference between a million and a billion.
